original_question: Does there exist a non-planar example of a unique full Steiner tree that has infinitely many branching points?
target_in_paper: Question 2.14 in Section 2.6 (Nonplanar explicit examples): "Can one construct a non-planar example of a unique full Steiner tree with infinitely many branching points?"
correct_elements: Your draft is already very close to the paper's official formulation. It correctly captures the four defining features of the target question: non-planarity, uniqueness, fullness, and infinitely many branching points. It also stays within the Steiner-tree setting and does not drift into a broader neighboring problem.
missing_details: The ambient setting should be Euclidean space R^d with d >= 3; the question belongs to the paper's Section 2.6 on nonplanar examples.
The tree should arise as the unique solution for some prescribed compact input set A, not as an abstract graph by itself.
A Steiner tree here means a closed set Sigma minimizing the one-dimensional Hausdorff measure H^1(Sigma) among all closed sets such that A union Sigma is connected.
Uniqueness means uniqueness of the Steiner minimizer for that same input set A.
Full means that every terminal point has degree 1.
Branching points mean Steiner points, i.e. nonterminal vertices of degree 3.
To make 'non-planar' stand alone, it should be stated that Sigma is not contained in any affine 2-plane.
The paper's phrasing is slightly more constructive than your draft: Section 2.6 asks whether one can construct such an example, not merely whether one exists.
The question does not restrict the input set A to be finite; in this part of the paper the intended setting allows compact inputs, including infinite ones.
refined_question: Can one construct a compact set A ⊂ R^d for some d >= 3 such that the Steiner problem for A—namely, minimizing H^1(Sigma) over closed sets Sigma with A ∪ Sigma connected—has a unique solution Sigma, where Sigma is full (every terminal point has degree 1), Sigma has infinitely many branching points (equivalently, infinitely many nonterminal degree-3 Steiner points), and Sigma is genuinely non-planar, i.e. not contained in any affine 2-plane?
justification: This draft targets Question 2.14, not the density-type questions in Section 2.3. The match is almost verbatim: the paper asks for a non-planar, unique, full Steiner tree with infinitely many branching points. The nearby context in Section 2.6 explains that the motivation is to go beyond the currently known planar explicit examples and to generalize the planar universal Steiner tree constructions. The definitions needed to make the question stand alone—Steiner tree, branching point, and full—are supplied in the opening paragraph of Section 2.
